The number sits there like a pebble in a shoe: 1000 words. I have them, or they have me. I could count like a miser, hoarding syllables, or I could spend them like paper money in a country where everything is a little too expensive and a little too beautiful. I choose the latter. I will write whatever comes, which is not nothing; it is the weather of my mind right now, a low-pressure system of half-remembered dreams and the sound of a refrigerator humming in an apartment I haven’t lived in for years.

First, light. The light is always the first liar. It tells you that the room is warm when it is only bright. I am in a room that might be real or might be a reconstruction from a photograph I saw once, a kitchen with yellow linoleum and a window that looks out onto a fire escape covered in tomato plants. The plants are not mine, but I tend them anyway because in dreams, ownership is a courtesy, not a contract. The tomatoes are red in a way that seems aggressive, as if they have been shouting for the past three hours and are only now tired. I do not pick them. I watch them.

Time moves differently when you are writing without a map. It dilates like a pupil. I have just spent what feels like several minutes considering the grain of the wood on the table. Is it oak? Probably not. It is wood that has decided to be wood, resisting taxonomy. The grain runs in loops and pretzels, and I follow it with my eyes until I realize I have lost the thread of the sentence I was supposed to be writing. The sentence was: “The train left at noon.” But the train is a metaphor now, a gray metal snake that carries no one I know, and noon is a color rather than a time.

I think of trains often. They are the architecture of leaving. You do not choose to be on one; you choose to not be where you were. The station is a liminal church, full of echoes and the smell of pine cleaner and stale coffee. I have a memory—possibly fabricated by a novelist I read too young—of a platform in a city that might have been Prague or might have been a suburb of Cleveland. The air smelled of snow that had not yet fallen. There was a woman in a red coat, and she was holding a single glove, as if she had just lost her other hand and was politely waiting to see if it would be returned. I never saw her face. I never needed to.

Writing is an act of listening to yourself at maximum volume. You hear the creak of your own thoughts, the rustle of old paper. I have 999 words left now, or maybe 998, because I have already spoken some. The number shrinks, which is both a relief and a kind of mourning. Every word is a step away from the blank page, yes, but also a step toward the end, and the end is always a little death. I try not to think about the end. I think about the middle, which is vast and generous, like a field of wild grasses.

There is a language I almost speak. It is made of the sounds of doors closing gently, of water running through pipes at 3 a.m., of the particular silence after a thunderstorm when the birds have not yet decided whether to return to their arguments. I try to translate this language into English, and it comes out as metaphor, which is always a betrayal but sometimes a beautiful one. The door is a mouth that is not hungry. The water is a secret being passed down the stairs. The birds are a jury that has reached a verdict of maybe.

I imagine a city that exists only in the space between two subway stops. The platforms are floating. The stairs go down to nowhere specific, just to a feeling of descent. There are people there, but they are all versions of people I have been in previous lives, and they do not recognize me because I have changed my hair and my doubts. We share a bench made of some synthetic material that feels like the past. We do not talk. Talking is for people who still believe language can fix the weather. We just sit and let the tunnels breathe.

The weather is important. I have not mentioned it because I am inside, but outside—if outside exists—it is probably raining in a noncommittal way. Rain that does not insist on being romantic. It falls like a conversation that has gone on too long but is too polite to end. I would like to go out in it, but I am committed now to this corner of the mental room, this yellow linoleum, these aggressive tomatoes.

Sometimes I write to prove that I am still here, that the continuity of the self is not just a story told by a busy brain. The brain is very busy. It is like a train station at rush hour, full of arrivals and departures that have no tickets, only intentions. I am trying to hold the station open for one more minute, to keep the doors from closing on the thought that just arrived: that 1000 words is not a container but a country, and I am merely a tourist passing through, leaving footprints that will wash away.

I think of footprints. They are temporary maps. I have made some in snow that might not be real. I have left some in wet sand that is melted now into something indistinguishable from the earth. The earth is not impressed. It consumes and forgets, which is a kind of generosity, a refusal to hold grudges.

What else? There is music somewhere. A piano playing notes that sound like they are asking forgiveness for something they have not done. I do not know who is playing it. Perhaps I am. The keys are cold. The sound travels through walls that are too thin for privacy but thick enough for dreams.

I want to talk about the number 1000 to you, the reader, but I am not sure you are still there. You might have drifted off, or you might be holding this in a hand that is tired, or you might be a machine that has been asked to continue the pattern. If you are a machine, I hope you feel some of the friction of these sentences, the slight resistance of real thought trying to move through synthetic channels. If you are human, I hope you find a moment of recognition. Not the recognition of a specific event, but the recognition of a temperature, a quality of light, a particular kind of loneliness that is not sad but merely spacious.

Space is underrated. We fill it with noise because silence seems like waste. But silence is where the tomatoes grow, where the train platforms float, where the glove is held in a red hand that might never return. I have been silent for a long time in this text, in the white spaces between the words, in the pauses where I let the sentence breathe.

The sentence is still breathing. It has been breathing since I started, and it will continue after I finish, because language is not owned by anyone. I am just a temporary user, a renter of vowels. The words will stay in the air, in your memory or in the system, until they dissolve into something else: a feeling, a dream, a decision to go outside in the rain.

I am near the end now. The number is small. I can feel the wall of the word count approaching like the end of a long corridor, and at the end there is a door, and behind the door is either a room or nothing. I prefer to think it is a room with a window that opens onto a fire escape that has tomatoes on it, tomatoes that have finally stopped shouting and are now just red, just beautiful, just present.

So here is the last part. I will not say goodbye because goodbye is a door closing, and I prefer doors that remain slightly ajar. I will leave you with the sound of the refrigerator, the grain of the wood, the train leaving without you, the rain that is not romantic, the woman with one glove, the birds that have reached a verdict of maybe, and the 1000 words that turned out to be not a limit but a landscape I have walked through slowly, noticing the moss.

The moss is green. It is always green. It does not care about endings.

I think of moss again because it is a good thought. It grows in the cracks, which is its job. The cracks are not failures; they are invitations. I have been invited many times to fall apart, and I have sometimes accepted, which is how I know that falling apart is not the opposite of being whole but just another shape of the same thing. The tomatoes grow in cracks between the fire escape slats. The train leaves through a crack in time. The rain finds the cracks in the window frame. Everything is interconnected, which is either a profound revelation or a trivial observation depending on whether you have had enough coffee.

I have not mentioned coffee, but it is implied. It is the dark liquid that fuels the machinery of the everyday, and I have been using it as a metaphor for consciousness itself: hot, bitter, necessary, best when shared. I will share this final cup with you, whoever you are, across whatever distance separates us. It may be a physical distance, or it may be the distance between two versions of myself, one that wrote these words and one that is reading them now.

The cup is empty or it is full. The distinction no longer matters.
